text:
With EFT (Emotional Freedom Techniques, or tapping), you tap gently on your body while you say something like, “Even though I have this anxiety, I am willing to be kind to the part of me that is afraid,” and you stay with what you feel. There isn’t a ton of evidence for EFT, but there are some studies on anxiety. A 2025 systematic review found 7 randomized controlled trials for anxiety disorders, and noted that EFT was more effective than no intervention in several of them, though it isn't one of the first-line therapies for anxiety.

If you would like more information about somatic experiencing, or even a free intro session for paid subscribers, please see my somatic guide. In somatic experiencing (SE), you are not digging into the trauma. You learn to track. So you might start by tracking, by discovering where the activation is, where a neutral place is, and then whether you can move your attention from one to the other, very slowly, like a snail.

Focusing is another approach where you work with your body. You might say to yourself, “What is the felt sense of this whole anxiety?” Don’t answer with your head; let your body come up with a vague sense of the whole anxiety. Then ask, “What would this felt sense like me to know?” Try a word or a phrase and see how well it fits the felt sense. But also see if what the word or phrase says is true of the situation. The word may feel ok, but say something that doesn’t fit the situation, or vice versa.
section: EFT Tapping / Somatic Experiencing / Gendlin Focusing (three sections of Appendix D: Anxiety, Body First, headings left out; the changed sentence opens Somatic Experiencing)
reader: Someone anxious who has done the breathing in Appendix D and is looking over three more body-first methods (tapping, somatic experiencing, focusing) to pick one to try alone or to learn with a person; they read the post on Substack, where some are paid subscribers and most are not.

placement: First sentence of 'Somatic Experiencing' (its heading is left out of this text), where the author's own sentence stands; nothing moved. opens.first_sentence: With EFT (Emotional Freedom Techniques, or tapping), you tap gently on your body while you say something like, “Even though I have this anxiety, I am willing to be kind to the part of me that is afraid,” and you stay with what you feel.
opens.why_reading: The text's first sentence opens 'EFT Tapping', the first of the three sections: it tells the anxious reader in one sentence what they would actually do with EFT (tap gently on the body, say a line that begins 'Even though I have this anxiety', stay with what they feel), so they can tell whether it is something they would try. The changed sentence opens the next section, 'Somatic Experiencing', on the author's pointer to his somatic guide.

fit.note: MISREAD read both ways. Without the three words, 'or even a free intro session' would have told me I could have one; with them I know it is for paid subscribers before I click. 'Free' beside 'paid' did not confuse on a quick read.

question_text.Q1: Why am I reading this sentence, and do I know it before I have to work through it? (the point first, in each sentence and each paragraph; a study after the question it answers; a term explained where it is first used, never in a sentence after it)
question_text.Q2: What is each instruction for, said in the reader's terms, and is it something the helper does ("have someone go with them"), not a rule stated as a fact ("someone goes with them")?
question_text.Q3: Which thing exactly? (pools of water, not water; any substance, not anything)
question_text.Q4: What does each word act on, or mean here? (adjunct remedy; known-genuine) Is every term a high-school graduate wouldn't know (enterocytes, BPC-157) explained once, where it is first used, and common ones (a vitamin) left alone? Is each mechanism explained by what it does in the reader's experience (dopamine "for motivation (by showing us what is important to pay attention to)"; DeltaFosB "preventing that learning from really clicking"), not by where it sits or what it looks like ("a chemical blanket", "the slower one underneath")? (E375)
question_text.Q5: Why does each sentence follow from the one before? (every but, so, because and this has what it turns on)
question_text.Q6: Is this the order the reader is thinking in, and does each idea sit next to what it continues?
question_text.Q7: Does each fact help this reader now, in their case (the same kind of thing they face, not just the same topic)?
question_text.Q8: Does each item belong in the group it is put in?
question_text.Q9: Is anything compressed? (one step a sentence, the small words that carry the relation, no space before mg)
